subject: Pulse check: steady-state vs burst metrics and action plan
messages:
From: Helen Park <helen.park@retailify.com>
To: Grace O'Connor <grace_oconnor@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 9 Apr 2028 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: Follow-up: performance targets and burst behavior (Retailify)

Thanks again for the demo today. Quick recap from our side and a few clarifying asks so we can align on sizing before the pilot: 

- SLO target: 95th latency for completed streaming responses should be <= 250ms for interactive flows; batch/async calls can be relaxed.
- Typical user journey: short prompts (50-120 tokens) for suggestion mode, but product search endpoint can spike with long prompts (avg ~420 tokens).
- Observed traffic pattern: steady-state ~70 QPS (primarily suggestions) with shopping event peaks reaching ~850 QPS for 45-60s bursts. These peaks tend to have heavier token use (avg 600 tokens).

We attached a small anonymized workload snapshot and sample request traces. Can you confirm the rough GPU footprint and whether Redwood's autoscaling + prefix caching can meet 95p SLO during peaks? Also: what telemetry we should send for the pilot (sample rates, essential fields)?

Attachment: retailify_workload_snapshot.csv (csv)

—Helen
Product Ops | Retailify
From: Grace O'Connor <grace_oconnor@redwood.ai>
To: Helen Park <helen.park@retailify.com>
Cc: Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 9 Apr 2028 17:04:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Follow-up: performance targets and burst behavior (Retailify)

Hi Helen — thanks for the clear recap and the sample. High level answers and next steps below, then Dylan/Marissa will add sizing detail and telemetry guidance.

High-level:
- 95p streaming latency <=250ms is achievable in most configurations for suggestion flows if we configure low-latency routing and enable prefix/KV caching for common completions.
- The 850 QPS 45-60s bursts with avg 600 tokens will need burst capacity planning (reserved burst pool + fast GPU warm paths) — otherwise you'll see queueing at the dispatcher.

Immediate asks for our sizing exercise:
1) Can you share a 24h window of request timestamps (even sampled) to confirm peak arrival curve?
2) Could you flag which endpoints require streaming vs non-streaming? (search suggestions = streaming, catalog enrichment = non-streaming)
3) Confirm typical arrival concurrency per user (single-session streaming vs multi-tab).

Planned deliverables (we'll produce a short sizing note + telemetry checklist):
- Sizing note with modeled QPS -> GPU reqs and tokens/sec -> budget impact (PDF).
- Telemetry/agent fields we need for pilot (headers for latency points, token counts, user/session id, sample id).
- Suggested canary plan and fallback policy (model variant + higher-latency fallback).

I added Dylan and Marissa to run the numbers and produce the PDF. Tentative follow-up: Wed 11 Apr 10:00 PT for a 30-min sizing walkthrough — does that work?

Thanks,
Grace
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference
From: Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwood.ai>
To: Grace O'Connor <grace_oconnor@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Cc: Helen Park <helen.park@retailify.com>
Date: Tue, 10 Apr 2028 09:18:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Follow-up: performance targets and burst behavior (Retailify)

Quick technical note before I run the model: a few clarifying Qs for Helen (copied Retailify):

- When you say 850 QPS peak for 45–60s, do you have the 1s-resolution timestamped counts? The burst shape (sharp spike vs ramp) changes queueing assumptions a lot.
- For streaming endpoints: what is the average token emission rate per second on the client (tokens/sec)? Are you using server-side streaming or client pulls per chunk?
- Any strict concurrency limit per API key / user that we should respect (we can model per-user throttles).

Assumptions I'll use unless you tell me otherwise: avg tokens/request = 420 (steady) / 600 (peak); tokens emitted at 30 tokens/sec on average for streaming responses; target 95p latency <=250ms (end-to-end streaming chunk arrival).

I'll produce two sizing scenarios: (A) conservative — reserve dedicated burst GPUs to hit 95p during peaks; (B) cost-optimized — opportunistic burst with autoscale and graceful tail latencies. Will attach the calcs.

—Dylan
Performance & SRE, Redwood Inference
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
To: Helen Park <helen.park@retailify.com>, Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwood.ai>, Grace O'Connor <grace_oconnor@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 10 Apr 2028 13:42:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Follow-up: performance targets and burst behavior (Retailify)

Helen — attached a short sizing note and the rough GPU footprint we modeled. Highlights below and action items.

Sizing highlights (rough):
- Steady-state: 70 QPS, avg 420 tokens/request -> ~29.4k tokens/sec aggregate -> 1 x A40-class fleet handling steady with headroom (with batching).
- Short spikes: 850 QPS at avg 600 tokens/request -> ~510k tokens/sec peak. To keep 95p streaming <=250ms we model:
   - Option 1 (SLA): 6 x A100-style GPUs in reserved burst pool + aggressive prefix caching. This gives enough concurrent decoding capacity to avoid dispatcher queueing for 60s bursts.
   - Option 2 (Cost-opt): autoscale to 4 x A100 with priority routing + ephemeral fallback to a slightly quantized variant for long tails (95p may increase to ~320–380ms under worst-case).

Telemetry checklist (minimal):
- request_id, user_id (hashed ok), endpoint, tokens_in, tokens_out, tokens/sec (client), arrival_timestamp_ms, model_variant, region, latency_ms (server + encode + network). Sample 1:100 for full traces, 1:10 for summary counters.

Attachments: redwood_sizing_notes.pdf (PDF) — contains the token/sec calcs, cost estimate, and canary run plan.

Next steps:
- Helen: confirm if you can provide 1s-resolution arrival counts for the last big event (we can accept 5% sampling).
- We will share the PDF and a 30-min walkthrough at Wed 11 Apr 10:00 PT.

Thanks — happy to iterate on the numbers.
Marissa
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
[attachment: redwood_sizing_notes.pdf]

Thanks all — the 10:00 PT slot on Wed works, and I'll extract the 1s-resolution counts for the last event (will deliver a sampled CSV by EOD today). One note: our streaming client uses server-push at ~25–30 tokens/sec; users commonly open multiple tabs during large promos (we can expect some degree of per-user concurrency).

We'll review Marissa's PDF ahead of the call. For the pilot, we want the conservative option (SLA-backed burst pool) — Retailify internal compliance needs a hard SLO for interactive search.

—Helen
